Real distribution systems carry unbalanced loads. The neutral conductor carries non-zero current, voltages shift from their balanced values, and the simple per-phase equivalent circuit no longer applies. Mastering unbalanced analysis is essential for load flow and power quality studies.

◆ Three-wire vs four-wire star

Four-wire (with neutral): Neutral wire keeps VN'N = 0. Each phase can be solved independently: Ia = VAN/Za, etc. The neutral current is IN = −(Ia + Ib + Ic) ≠ 0.

Three-wire (no neutral): The load neutral N' shifts away from the supply neutral N. Millman's theorem (node voltage method) gives VN'N directly.

◆ Millman's theorem for the load neutral voltage

VN'N = (VANYa + VBNYb + VCNYc) / (Ya + Yb + Yc)
where Yx = 1/Zx (load admittances)

Phase voltages across the loads: Va = VAN − VN'N, etc.

◆ Worked numerical

Supply: 400 V (line), balanced, positive sequence. Loads (star): Za = 10∠0° Ω, Zb = 10∠30° Ω, Zc = 10∠−30° Ω.

VAN = (400/√3)∠0° = 231∠0° V; VBN = 231∠−120°; VCN = 231∠120°.
Ya = 0.1∠0°, Yb = 0.1∠−30°, Yc = 0.1∠30°.
Numerator: 231×0.1∠0° + 231×0.1∠(−150°) + 231×0.1∠(90°).
= 23.1∠0° + 23.1∠−150° + 23.1∠90°.
≈ 23.1 + (−20.0 − j11.55) + (j23.1) = 3.1 + j11.55 = 11.96∠75°.
Denominator: 0.3∠0° + 0.1∠−30° + 0.1∠30° = 0.3 + 0.1(cos30° − jsin30°) + 0.1(cos30° + jsin30°) = 0.3 + 0.2cos30° = 0.3 + 0.1732 = 0.4732∠0°.
VN'N = 11.96∠75°/0.4732 = 25.3∠75° V.

This neutral shift changes the actual phase voltages across each load branch — some phases see more voltage, others less.

◆ Four-wire case — neutral current

IN = −(Ia + Ib + Ic)

In a balanced system IN = 0 exactly; in an unbalanced system it can be large, overloading the neutral conductor if it is undersized.

Common mistake: Applying the simple balanced per-phase formula (Vphase = Vline/√3) to each phase load in an unbalanced three-wire system. The phase voltage is no longer Vline/√3 because the neutral has shifted.
Placement trap: "The neutral current equals Ia + Ib + Ic." — It is the negative of that sum. The neutral carries return current.

◆ Practical notes

  • Domestic loads (single-phase appliances distributed across phases) are the primary cause of star-system imbalance.
  • An open-neutral in a three-wire star system subjects individual loads to voltage levels anywhere from near-zero to line voltage — dangerous.
  • The neutral wire must be sized for the worst-case unbalanced neutral current, not as an afterthought.

◆ Interview question

"Why is the neutral conductor sometimes thicker than the phase conductors in LT distribution?" — In the presence of non-linear single-phase loads (switch-mode power supplies, dimmers), the triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, …) add rather than cancel in the neutral. The neutral can carry up to √3 times the phase current, requiring a conductor at least as large as the phase conductor.

Industrial loads (large motors, furnaces) are often connected in delta. An unbalanced delta has unequal phase currents and line currents that do not form a balanced set, affecting supply-side voltage regulation and protection settings.

◆ Delta circuit basics (reminder)

In a delta, each load impedance Zab, Zbc, Zca is connected directly across a line-to-line voltage. The line-to-line voltages are fixed by the source (assuming a stiff source), regardless of the load.

Phase currents (delta load):
Iab = VAB/Zab,   Ibc = VBC/Zbc,   Ica = VCA/Zca

Line currents by KCL at each node:

IA = Iab − Ica
IB = Ibc − Iab
IC = Ica − Ibc

Check: IA + IB + IC = 0 always (no neutral in delta).

◆ Worked numerical

Supply: 400 V (line-to-line), balanced. Delta loads: Zab = 10∠0° Ω, Zbc = 20∠0° Ω, Zca = 10∠90° Ω.

VAB = 400∠0°, VBC = 400∠−120°, VCA = 400∠120°.
Iab = 400∠0°/10 = 40∠0° A.
Ibc = 400∠−120°/20 = 20∠−120° A.
Ica = 400∠120°/(10∠90°) = 40∠30° A.
IA = 40∠0° − 40∠30° = 40 − (34.64 + j20) = 5.36 − j20 = 20.7∠−75° A.
IB = 20∠−120° − 40∠0° = (−10 − j17.32) − 40 = −50 − j17.32 = 52.9∠−199° A.
IC = 40∠30° − 20∠−120° = (34.64 + j20) − (−10 − j17.32) = 44.64 + j37.32 = 58.2∠39.9° A.

◆ Key differences: unbalanced delta vs unbalanced star

FeatureUnbalanced StarUnbalanced Delta
Phase voltagesShift with neutral displacementFixed by line voltage (source stiff)
Phase currentsEasy to find once VN'N knownDirect: VLL/Zbranch
Line currentsEqual to phase currentsPhasor difference of two phase currents
Neutral currentNon-zero in 4-wire; zero in 3-wireNo neutral; IA+IB+IC=0
Common mistake: Assuming the line current equals the delta phase current in magnitude (i.e., multiplying by √3). The √3 relationship only holds when the three phase currents form a balanced set.
Placement trap: "In an unbalanced delta, Iline = √3 × Iphase." — False. This is a balanced-only result.

◆ Interview question

"What happens to a delta-connected load when one phase of the supply is lost?" — Two delta branches still receive voltage (one across the remaining healthy line, one via a series path through the third branch). The currents redistribute unequally. The branch across the missing voltage carries current only by induction from the others — this is a significant cause of motor overheating on single-phasing (two-phase supply).

In an unbalanced three-wire star load, the load neutral N' does not coincide with the supply neutral N. The phasor voltage VN'N is the neutral shift voltage (also called neutral displacement voltage). It modifies the actual phase voltage each load receives.

VN'N = (VAN/Za + VBN/Zb + VCN/Zc) / (1/Za + 1/Zb + 1/Zc)

Once VN'N is known: Va = VAN − VN'N, Vb = VBN − VN'N, Vc = VCN − VN'N.

◆ Physical interpretation

Imagine the three supply phasors VAN, VBN, VCN as three ropes pulling the load neutral N'. Equal ropes pull N' to the geometric centre (N). Unequal impedances mean unequal tensions, so N' shifts toward the phase with the largest admittance (smallest impedance).

◆ Extreme case — one phase open

If phase C is open-circuited (Zc → ∞, Yc = 0), then:
VN'N = (VANYa + VBNYb)/(Ya + Yb).
The load neutral now lies on the line joining the tip of VAN and VBN weighted by the admittances. Phase C load sees VCN − VN'N, which can be nearly equal to a line voltage!

◆ Extreme case — one phase short-circuited

If Za → 0 (short circuit), Ya → ∞, then VN'N → VAN. The load neutral is pulled all the way to the tip of the A-phase phasor. Phases B and C now see full line-to-line voltages instead of their normal phase voltages — highly dangerous for equipment rated at phase voltage.

◆ Worked example

400 V balanced supply, three-wire star load: Za = 5 Ω, Zb = 10∠30° Ω, Zc = open.

VN'N = (231∠0°/5 + 231∠−120°/10∠30°) / (1/5 + 1/10∠30°)
= (46.2∠0° + 23.1∠−150°) / (0.2 + 0.1∠−30°)
Numerator: 46.2 + 23.1(cos150°−jsin150°) = 46.2 − 20.01 − j11.55 = 26.19 − j11.55 = 28.62∠−23.8°.
Denominator: 0.2 + 0.1(0.866−j0.5) = 0.2867 − j0.05 = 0.291∠−9.9°.
VN'N = 28.62∠−23.8° / 0.291∠−9.9° = 98.3∠−13.9° V.

This is 98.3 V of neutral shift — phase C load (open) sees VCN−VN'N = 231∠120° − 98.3∠−13.9°. In a domestic context, this extra voltage would damage appliances on phase C.

Common mistake: Applying Millman's theorem to a four-wire system. In a four-wire system VN'N = 0 by definition (the neutral wire enforces it); Millman applies only to three-wire star.
Placement trap: "Neutral shift is the same as a phase imbalance in the supply." — Neutral shift is caused by load imbalance; supply imbalance is a separate phenomenon. Both can coexist.

◆ Interview question

"Why does an open neutral in a LT distribution feeder cause equipment damage?" — Without the neutral conductor, VN'N is no longer clamped to zero. With asymmetric single-phase loads, the neutral shifts towards the heavier loaded phase: loads on that phase see a reduced voltage while loads on the lightly loaded phase see a much higher voltage than designed. The 230 V rated equipment on the high-voltage phase can receive close to 400 V, causing insulation failure and burnout.

Every utility bill depends on power factor. Equipment ratings, cable sizes and transformer capacities are all determined by apparent power. Power factor correction (PFC) reduces reactive current, cutting I²R losses and releasing capacity in the distribution system.

◆ Definitions and formulas

S = P + jQ   (complex power, VA)
P = Real{S} = Vrms·Irms·cos φ   (active power, W)
Q = Imag{S} = Vrms·Irms·sin φ   (reactive power, VAR)
|S| = Vrms·Irms   (apparent power, VA)
pf = cos φ = P/|S|
S = V·I*   (phasor product, I conjugated)

◆ Power triangle

|S|² = P² + Q². For an inductive load Q > 0, S lies in the first quadrant (lagging). For a capacitive load Q < 0, S lies in the fourth quadrant (leading).

◆ Power in three-phase circuits

P3φ = √3·VL·IL·cos φ   (balanced)
Q3φ = √3·VL·IL·sin φ
S3φ = √3·VL·IL
Complex: S3φ = 3·Vph·Iph* = P3φ + jQ3φ

For an unbalanced system: Stotal = VaIa* + VbIb* + VcIc*.

◆ Power factor correction

To correct a lagging load from pf1 to pf2 (target, > pf1), add a shunt capacitor across the load.

QC = P(tan φ1 − tan φ2)
C = QC/(ω·Vrms²)   (single-phase)
C = QC/(ω·VL²)   (three-phase, star connection, per-phase)
Cdelta = QC/(3ω·VL²)   (three-phase, delta connection)

◆ Worked numerical

A 400 V (line), 50 Hz, balanced 3φ load absorbs 120 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. Correct to 0.95 pf lagging.

φ₁ = cos⁻¹(0.6) = 53.13°, tan φ₁ = 1.333.
φ₂ = cos⁻¹(0.95) = 18.19°, tan φ₂ = 0.329.
QC = 120 k × (1.333 − 0.329) = 120 × 1.004 = 120.5 kVAR.
Before: |S₁| = 120/0.6 = 200 kVA, IL = 200 000/(√3 × 400) = 289 A.
After: |S₂| = 120/0.95 = 126.3 kVA, IL = 126 300/(√3 × 400) = 182 A — a 37 % reduction in line current!
C (star, per phase) = 120 500/(3 × 2π × 50 × (400/√3)²) = 120 500/(3 × 314.16 × 53 333) = 2.40 × 10⁻³ F = 2.40 mF (per phase).
Or C (delta) = 2.40 m/3 = 0.80 mF per delta branch.

◆ Over-correction warning

Adding too large a capacitor drives the power factor leading. The line current rises again. Utilities may penalise leading power factor as well as lagging. Optimal correction is unity or just lagging.

Common mistake: Using S = V·I instead of S = V·I* (conjugate). If V = V∠0° and I = I∠−φ (lagging), then S = V∠0° × I∠+φ = VI∠φ, giving positive Q (inductive). Forgetting the conjugate reverses the sign of Q.
Placement trap: "Power factor = cos(voltage angle − current angle)." — True, but always identify which angle leads. pf is the same regardless of reference, but the sign of Q (leading vs lagging) requires knowing which phasor is ahead.

◆ Interview question

"Why does power factor correction reduce feeder losses even though the real power consumed is unchanged?" — The feeder carries apparent current. At lower power factor the same real power requires a larger current (I = P/(√3·V·pf)). Copper loss I²R therefore falls as the square of the current improvement. Correction from 0.6 to 0.95 reduces current by ~37 %, cutting I²R losses by ~57 %.

Every amplifier, filter, transmission line, and power network is modelled as a two-port. The Z and Y parameter sets are the foundation for all other two-port descriptions and for circuit interconnection analysis.

◆ Driving-Point Functions

A driving-point function (DPF) is an immittance (impedance or admittance) measured at a single port with all other independent sources set to zero.

FunctionDefinitionUnit
Driving-point impedanceZ(s) = V(s) / I(s)Ω
Driving-point admittanceY(s) = I(s) / V(s)S (siemens)

Conditions for a valid DPF (positive-real function):

  • Poles and zeros are in the left half of the s-plane or on the jω-axis.
  • Poles on the jω-axis are simple with real, positive residues.
  • Re[Z(jω)] ≥ 0 for all ω (passive network — cannot deliver energy).

◆ The Two-Port Network

A two-port has Port 1 (input: V₁, I₁) and Port 2 (output: V₂, I₂). By convention, currents I₁ and I₂ both point into the port. There is no direct connection between the two ports for an ideal two-port; only the network inside couples them.

◆ Z Parameters (Open-Circuit Impedance Parameters)

The Z-parameter set expresses port voltages in terms of port currents:

V₁ = Z₁₁ I₁ + Z₁₂ I₂
V₂ = Z₂₁ I₁ + Z₂₂ I₂

Individual parameters (measured with one port open-circuited):

ParameterMeasurement conditionFormulaName
Z₁₁I₂ = 0 (Port 2 open)V₁/I₁Input driving-point impedance
Z₁₂I₁ = 0 (Port 1 open)V₁/I₂Reverse transfer impedance
Z₂₁I₂ = 0 (Port 2 open)V₂/I₁Forward transfer impedance
Z₂₂I₁ = 0 (Port 1 open)V₂/I₂Output driving-point impedance

T-equivalent circuit for Z parameters: The two-port is represented by a π-of-T topology with series elements (Z₁₁−Z₁₂) on each port arm and a shunt element Z₁₂ in the middle (valid only for reciprocal networks where Z₁₂ = Z₂₁).

◆ Y Parameters (Short-Circuit Admittance Parameters)

The Y-parameter set expresses port currents in terms of port voltages:

I₁ = Y₁₁ V₁ + Y₁₂ V₂
I₂ = Y₂₁ V₁ + Y₂₂ V₂
ParameterMeasurement conditionFormulaName
Y₁₁V₂ = 0 (Port 2 short)I₁/V₁Input short-circuit admittance
Y₁₂V₁ = 0 (Port 1 short)I₁/V₂Reverse transfer admittance
Y₂₁V₂ = 0 (Port 2 short)I₂/V₁Forward transfer admittance
Y₂₂V₁ = 0 (Port 1 short)I₂/V₂Output short-circuit admittance

π-equivalent circuit for Y parameters: Shunt admittances (Y₁₁+Y₁₂) and (Y₂₂+Y₁₂) at each port and a shunt element (−Y₁₂) in the middle (reciprocal network).

◆ Relationship between Z and Y

[Y] = [Z]⁻¹   ⟺   [Z] = [Y]⁻¹

This inverse exists only if det([Z]) ≠ 0. Not all two-ports have both Z and Y parameters (e.g., ideal transformer has no Z matrix).

◆ Worked Example — Z Parameters of a T-Network

A T-network has Z_a in the input arm, Z_b in the output arm, and Z_c as the shunt element.

  • Z₁₁ = Z_a + Z_c (Port 2 open: see both arms from Port 1)
  • Z₂₂ = Z_b + Z_c (Port 1 open)
  • Z₁₂ = Z₂₁ = Z_c (only the shunt element is common — reciprocity)

Numerical: Z_a = 2 Ω, Z_b = 3 Ω, Z_c = 5 Ω ⟹ Z₁₁=7, Z₂₂=8, Z₁₂=Z₂₁=5 Ω.

◆ Practical Applications

  • Amplifier small-signal modelling (Z parameters for transistor).
  • Filter synthesis (ladder networks described by Y parameters).
  • Impedance matching networks (power transfer analysis).
  • Network analyser measurements at RF frequencies.

◆ Common Mistakes

  • Placement Trap: Z parameters are measured with ports open; Y parameters with ports short-circuited. Mixing the two is a common error.
  • Forgetting the sign convention: I₁ and I₂ both enter the network (positive into the port).
  • Assuming Z and Y always exist — ideal transformer and series connection of ideal sources may not have a defined Z or Y matrix.

◆ Quick Revision

  • Z: V = Z·I, open-circuit measurement, T-equivalent.
  • Y: I = Y·V, short-circuit measurement, π-equivalent.
  • Reciprocal: Z₁₂=Z₂₁, Y₁₂=Y₂₁.
  • Symmetric: Z₁₁=Z₂₂, Y₁₁=Y₂₂ (also reciprocal).
  • [Y] = [Z]⁻¹.

Transistors are most conveniently characterised by h parameters (mixed voltage-current). Cascaded networks (amplifier stages, filters, transmission lines) are most conveniently analysed using the ABCD (T) matrix because cascade simply multiplies matrices. Knowing conditions for symmetry and reciprocity is essential for simplifying analysis.

◆ h Parameters (Hybrid Parameters)

h parameters mix port variables — Port 1 current and Port 2 voltage are the independent variables:

V₁ = h₁₁ I₁ + h₁₂ V₂
I₂ = h₂₁ I₁ + h₂₂ V₂
ParameterConditionFormulaPhysical meaning
h₁₁V₂ = 0V₁/I₁Input impedance (Port 2 shorted) [Ω]
h₁₂I₁ = 0V₁/V₂Reverse voltage transfer ratio [dimensionless]
h₂₁V₂ = 0I₂/I₁Forward current transfer ratio (β for BJT) [dimensionless]
h₂₂I₁ = 0I₂/V₂Output admittance (Port 1 open) [S]

BJT small-signal model: h₁₁ = hᵢₑ (input impedance), h₁₂ = hᵣₑ (reverse feedback ratio), h₂₁ = hfₑ (current gain ≈ β), h₂₂ = hoₑ (output admittance).

◆ T (ABCD) Parameters — Transmission Matrix

ABCD parameters relate the input port quantities to the output port quantities. Note the output current I₂ is defined as leaving Port 2 (opposite convention from Z/Y/h):

V₁ = A V₂ − B I₂
I₁ = C V₂ − D I₂
ParameterConditionFormulaPhysical meaning
AI₂ = 0 (Port 2 open)V₁/V₂Reverse open-circuit voltage ratio [dimensionless]
BV₂ = 0 (Port 2 short)−V₁/I₂Reverse short-circuit transfer impedance [Ω]
CI₂ = 0 (Port 2 open)I₁/V₂Reverse open-circuit transfer admittance [S]
DV₂ = 0 (Port 2 short)−I₁/I₂Reverse short-circuit current ratio [dimensionless]

Key property of cascade: If Network 1 has matrix [T₁] and Network 2 has matrix [T₂], the cascade (output of N1 connected to input of N2) has overall matrix [T] = [T₁][T₂]. This is the main advantage of ABCD parameters.

◆ Conditions for Reciprocity and Symmetry

A two-port is reciprocal if it contains only passive bilateral elements (R, L, C, M) — no dependent sources, no active elements.

A two-port is symmetric if it is also geometrically symmetric (Port 1 and Port 2 are interchangeable).

Parameter setReciprocity conditionSymmetry condition
ZZ₁₂ = Z₂₁Z₁₁ = Z₂₂ and Z₁₂ = Z₂₁
YY₁₂ = Y₂₁Y₁₁ = Y₂₂ and Y₁₂ = Y₂₁
hh₁₂ = −h₂₁h₁₁ h₂₂ − h₁₂ h₂₁ = 1 and h₁₂ = −h₂₁
ABCD (T)AD − BC = 1A = D and AD − BC = 1

Physical check — reciprocity: In a reciprocal network, swapping excitation and response ports gives the same transfer ratio. Formally: Z₁₂ = Z₂₁ (Lorentz reciprocity theorem for passive networks).

◆ Relationships between Parameter Sets

Any parameter set can be derived from any other by algebraic manipulation. Two commonly needed conversions:

ConversionKey relations
Z → hh₁₁ = ΔZ/Z₂₂, h₁₂ = Z₁₂/Z₂₂, h₂₁ = −Z₂₁/Z₂₂, h₂₂ = 1/Z₂₂   (ΔZ = Z₁₁Z₂₂ − Z₁₂Z₂₁)
Z → ABCDA = Z₁₁/Z₂₁, B = ΔZ/Z₂₁, C = 1/Z₂₁, D = Z₂₂/Z₂₁

◆ Worked Example — ABCD of a Simple Series Impedance

For a single series impedance Z in the signal path (no shunt element):

  • A = 1, B = Z, C = 0, D = 1
  • AD − BC = 1·1 − Z·0 = 1 ✓ (reciprocal)
  • A = D ✓ (symmetric — a symmetric series element)

Numerical: Z = j10 Ω (inductor at some frequency): A=1, B=j10, C=0, D=1. AD−BC = 1. ✓

◆ Practical Applications

  • h parameters: transistor datasheet characterisation and amplifier analysis.
  • ABCD matrix: transmission line sections, multi-stage filter cascades, optical element cascades.
  • Symmetry conditions: balun design, differential amplifier input stage verification.
  • Reciprocity check: antenna coupling coefficients, network analyser calibration.

◆ Common Mistakes

  • Placement Trap: In the ABCD matrix, I₂ is defined as leaving Port 2 (negative convention), unlike Z/Y/h where I₂ enters. This sign difference is the most common source of error when converting between parameter sets.
  • Confusing reciprocity (Z₁₂=Z₂₁) with symmetry (Z₁₁=Z₂₂). Reciprocity does not imply symmetry.
  • Applying cascade multiplication in the wrong order: [T] = [T₁][T₂] means N1 input feeds N2. Reversing the order gives a wrong result.

◆ Quick Revision

  • h params: mixed (V₁,I₂) as outputs; h₂₁ = current gain; BJT model.
  • ABCD: input variables = output variables; cascade → matrix multiply.
  • Reciprocal: Z₁₂=Z₂₁ / Y₁₂=Y₂₁ / h₁₂=−h₂₁ / AD−BC=1.
  • Symmetric: additionally Z₁₁=Z₂₂ / Y₁₁=Y₂₂ / A=D.

Real systems combine multiple two-port blocks. The type of interconnection (series, parallel, cascade) determines which parameter set is most convenient. T-π transformation is a fundamental tool used in network equivalents and impedance matching.

◆ Types of Two-Port Interconnections

InterconnectionWhat is combinedConvenient parameterRule
Series-series (Series at both ports)Port 1 in series; Port 2 in seriesZ parameters[Z] = [Z₁] + [Z₂]
Parallel-parallel (Shunt at both ports)Port 1 in parallel; Port 2 in parallelY parameters[Y] = [Y₁] + [Y₂]
Cascade (output of N1 → input of N2)Output port feeds next input portABCD parameters[T] = [T₁] · [T₂]
Series-parallel (Port 1 series, Port 2 parallel)Mixedh parameters[h] = [h₁] + [h₂]
Parallel-series (Port 1 parallel, Port 2 series)Mixedg (inverse-h) parameters[g] = [g₁] + [g₂]

Portability condition: When networks are interconnected, the port currents must still satisfy port conditions (I entering one terminal equals I leaving the other). If this is violated (e.g., due to common ground loops), the combined parameter matrix is not simply the sum/product — the Brune test must be applied.

◆ Series-Series Interconnection (Z parameters)

When input ports are connected in series and output ports in series:

[Z_total] = [Z_A] + [Z_B]

Each Z parameter of the combined network is the sum of the corresponding Z parameters of the individual networks. This is because the same current flows through each network and voltages add.

◆ Parallel-Parallel Interconnection (Y parameters)

When input ports are connected in parallel and output ports in parallel:

[Y_total] = [Y_A] + [Y_B]

The same voltage appears across each network, and currents add — so admittances add.

◆ Cascade Interconnection (ABCD parameters)

The output port of Network A drives the input port of Network B:

[T_total] = [T_A] · [T_B]

Matrix multiplication (not element-by-element addition). For n cascaded stages: [T] = [T₁][T₂]...[Tₙ].

Example — two cascaded series impedances Z₁ and Z₂:

[T₁] = [[1, Z₁],[0, 1]], [T₂] = [[1, Z₂],[0, 1]]

[T] = [[1, Z₁+Z₂],[0, 1]] → equivalent to a single series impedance Z₁+Z₂. ✓

◆ T-π (Star-Delta) Transformation

The T-π transformation (also called star-delta or Y-Δ conversion) converts a three-terminal network between its T-form (star/Y) and π-form (delta/Δ). It is used to simplify networks that cannot be reduced by series/parallel rules.

T (Star) → π (Delta) conversion:

Z_ab = Z_a + Z_b + (Z_a · Z_b)/Z_c
Z_bc = Z_b + Z_c + (Z_b · Z_c)/Z_a
Z_ca = Z_c + Z_a + (Z_c · Z_a)/Z_b

where Z_a, Z_b, Z_c are the three arms of the T (with Z_c as the shunt/common arm) and Z_ab, Z_bc, Z_ca are the three arms of the equivalent π.

π (Delta) → T (Star) conversion:

Z_a = (Z_ab · Z_ca) / (Z_ab + Z_bc + Z_ca)
Z_b = (Z_ab · Z_bc) / (Z_ab + Z_bc + Z_ca)
Z_c = (Z_bc · Z_ca) / (Z_ab + Z_bc + Z_ca)

Note the pattern: each star arm = (product of two adjacent delta arms) / (sum of all three delta arms).

◆ Worked Example — Cascade of T-Network and π-Network

Network A (T-form): Z_a=j2, Z_b=j2, Z_c=−j4. ABCD: A=1+Z_a/Z_c, B=Z_a+Z_b+Z_aZ_b/Z_c, C=1/Z_c, D=1+Z_b/Z_c.

A = 1 + j2/(−j4) = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, D = 0.5 by symmetry, C = 1/(−j4) = j0.25, B = j2+j2+(j2)(j2)/(−j4) = j4 + (−4)/(−j4) = j4 − j1 = j3.

Check: AD−BC = 0.5×0.5 − j3×j0.25 = 0.25 + 0.75 = 1 ✓ (reciprocal and symmetric).

◆ Practical Applications

  • Cascade analysis: multi-stage amplifiers, ladder filters, optical element trains.
  • T-π transformation: three-phase load balancing, power system bus impedance reduction, Wheatstone bridge analysis.
  • Series-parallel interconnection: feedback amplifier analysis using h parameters.
  • Transmission line sections: ABCD cascade of distributed sections.

◆ Common Mistakes

  • Placement Trap: For cascade, use matrix multiplication [T] = [T₁][T₂]. For series-series, use matrix addition [Z] = [Z₁]+[Z₂]. Mixing these up is the most frequent exam error.
  • In T→π conversion: the formula for each delta arm uses the product of the two adjacent star arms divided by the opposite star arm, then adds the two adjacent arms. The pattern "product over opposite" is easy to remember.
  • Violating port conditions when interconnecting: both networks must share a common ground for the parallel-parallel connection to be valid. A separate grounding wire can invalidate the port condition.

◆ Quick Revision

  • Series-series → add [Z].
  • Parallel-parallel → add [Y].
  • Cascade → multiply [T] = [T₁][T₂].
  • T→π: each delta arm = (adj × adj) / opp + adj + adj.
  • π→T: each star arm = (adj × adj) / (sum of all delta).

Electrical filters are frequency-selective two-port networks that pass desired frequency bands with negligible attenuation while suppressing unwanted frequencies. From removing 50 Hz power supply hum in audio equipment to selecting radio stations and preventing anti-aliasing in DSP systems, filter theory forms the bedrock of communication and signal processing engineering.

◆ 1. Filter Classifications

Filter TypePassband RangeStopband RangeTypical Application
Low-Pass Filter (LPF)$0 \le f \le f_c$$f > f_c$Anti-aliasing in ADC, DC power supply ripple reduction
High-Pass Filter (HPF)$f \ge f_c$$0 \le f < f_c$Audio tweeters, DC blocking, RF antenna coupling
Band-Pass Filter (BPF)$f_{c1} \le f \le f_{c2}$$f < f_{c1}$ and $f > f_{c2}$Radio/TV station tuning, IF amplifiers
Band-Stop / Notch Filter (BSF)$f < f_{c1}$ and $f > f_{c2}$$f_{c1} \le f \le f_{c2}$50/60 Hz power-line hum rejection

◆ 2. Propagation Constant and Attenuation Units

For a symmetrical two-port filter section terminated in its characteristic impedance $Z_0$, the ratio of input current $I_1$ to output current $I_2$ defines the propagation constant $\\gamma$:

$$\\frac{I_1}{I_2} = e^\\gamma = e^{\\alpha + j\\beta} = e^\\alpha \\angle \\beta$$
  • Attenuation Constant $\\alpha$: Defines reduction in magnitude. $\\alpha = \\ln|I_1/I_2|$ in Nepers (Np).
  • Phase Constant $\\beta$: Defines phase change in radians. $\\beta = \\angle(I_1) - \\angle(I_2)$.
  • Decibels (dB): Attenuation in decibels is $\\text{dB} = 20 \log_{10}|I_1/I_2| = 20 \log_{10}(e^\\alpha) = 20 \\alpha \log_{10}(e) \\approx 8.686 \\alpha$.
  • Conversion: $1\\text{ Neper} \\approx 8.686\\text{ dB}$, and $1\\text{ dB} \\approx 0.1151\\text{ Neper}$.

◆ 3. Passband and Stopband Conditions

For a symmetrical reactive T or $\\pi$ section with series arm impedance $Z_1$ and shunt arm impedance $Z_2$:

$$\\cosh\\gamma = 1 + \\frac{Z_1}{2Z_2}$$

Since $\\cosh(\\alpha + j\\beta) = \\cosh\\alpha \\cos\\beta + j\\sinh\\alpha \\sin\\beta$, for a purely reactive lossless network ($Z_1, Z_2$ purely imaginary, so $Z_1/Z_2$ is real):

  • Passband (Zero Attenuation, $\\alpha = 0$): $\\cosh\\gamma = \\cos\\beta$. Since $-1 \le \\cos\\beta \le +1$:
    $$-1 \le 1 + \\frac{Z_1}{2Z_2} \le +1 \implies -1 \le \\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} \le 0$$
  • Stopband (Attenuation $\\alpha > 0$): Occurs when $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} < -1$ or $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} > 0$.
  • Cutoff Frequencies: Marked by the boundaries where $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} = 0$ and $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} = -1$.

◆ 4. Characteristic Impedance ($Z_0$)

The characteristic impedance of symmetrical T and $\\pi$ sections are related to open-circuit and short-circuit impedances ($Z_0 = \\sqrt{Z_{oc} Z_{sc}}$):

$$Z_{0T} = \\sqrt{Z_1 Z_2 \\left(1 + \\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2}\\right)}, \\qquad Z_{0\\pi} = \\frac{\\sqrt{Z_1 Z_2}}{\\sqrt{1 + \\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2}}}$$

Notice the fundamental identity: $Z_{0T} \\cdot Z_{0\\pi} = Z_1 Z_2 = k^2 = R_0^2$.

In the passband ($-1 < Z_1/(4Z_2) < 0$), $Z_{0T}$ and $Z_{0\\pi}$ are purely real (resistive), allowing transmission of active power without reflection. In the stopband, $Z_0$ becomes purely imaginary (reactive), reflecting incident energy back toward the source.

◆ 5. Constant-k Filter Concept

A filter in which the series arm impedance $Z_1$ and shunt arm impedance $Z_2$ satisfy:

$$Z_1 \\cdot Z_2 = k^2 = R_0^2 = \\text{constant (independent of frequency)}$$

is called a constant-k filter (or prototype filter). $R_0$ is the nominal characteristic impedance in the passband at zero or infinite frequency.

◆ Worked Example: Transmission Verification

Problem: A symmetrical T-network has series arm impedance $Z_1 = j100\,\\Omega$ and shunt arm impedance $Z_2 = -j200\,\\Omega$. Determine if the operating frequency is in the passband, and calculate $Z_{0T}$.

Solution:
Ratio $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} = \\frac{j100}{4(-j200)} = \\frac{100}{-800} = -0.125$.
Since $-1 < -0.125 < 0$, the network operates in the passband ($\\alpha = 0$).
Product $Z_1 Z_2 = (j100)(-j200) = 20000\,\\Omega^2$.
$Z_{0T} = \\sqrt{Z_1 Z_2 (1 + Z_1/(4Z_2))} = \\sqrt{20000 \\times (1 - 0.125)} = \\sqrt{20000 \\times 0.875} = \\sqrt{17500} \\approx 132.29\,\\Omega$.
Because it is purely real and positive, power is transmitted without resistive loss. ✓

Common mistake: Confusing the full series arm impedance $Z_1$ with the individual branch elements in a symmetrical T-section ($Z_1/2$). The ratio condition is always $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2}$, where $Z_1$ is the total series branch impedance.
Placement trap: "In an ideal lossless filter passband, does the signal undergo attenuation or phase shift?" — In the passband, attenuation $\\alpha = 0$ (zero loss), but phase shift $\\beta \ne 0$ varies continuously with frequency across the band.

◆ Interview Questions

"What is the physical meaning of characteristic impedance in filter networks?" — $Z_0$ is the impedance looking into the input port of a filter section when its output port is terminated in the same impedance $Z_0$. Terminating in $Z_0$ eliminates reflections at the junction, ensuring maximum power transfer across the passband.

While constant-k prototype filters are simple to design, they suffer from two major real-world flaws: a sluggish attenuation rate immediately outside the passband, and a characteristic impedance that varies drastically with frequency. The m-derived filter (introduced by Otto Zobel) completely solves both problems by placing an infinite attenuation notch right next to the cutoff frequency and providing a nearly flat input impedance across 85% of the passband.

◆ 1. Constant-k Prototype Low-Pass Filter (LPF)

In a constant-k LPF, the series arm is an inductor ($Z_1 = j\\omega L$) and the shunt arm is a capacitor ($Z_2 = 1/(j\\omega C)$).
Then $Z_1 Z_2 = (j\\omega L)(1/j\\omega C) = L/C = R_0^2 = k^2$.

$$\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} = \\frac{j\\omega L}{4/(j\\omega C)} = -\\frac{\\omega^2 LC}{4}$$

At the cutoff boundary, $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} = -1 \implies \\frac{\\omega_c^2 LC}{4} = 1 \implies \\omega_c = \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{LC}}$:

$$f_c = \\frac{1}{\\pi \\sqrt{LC}}, \\qquad R_0 = \\sqrt{\\frac{L}{C}}$$

Design Formulas for Prototype LPF:

$$L = \\frac{R_0}{\\pi f_c}, \\qquad C = \\frac{1}{\\pi f_c R_0}$$

For a symmetrical T-section, each series inductor is $L/2$ and the shunt capacitor is $C$. For a $\\pi$-section, the series inductor is $L$ and each shunt capacitor is $C/2$.

Passband impedance variation: $Z_{0T} = R_0 \\sqrt{1 - (f/f_c)^2}$, and $Z_{0\\pi} = \\frac{R_0}{\\sqrt{1 - (f/f_c)^2}}$.

◆ 2. Constant-k Prototype High-Pass Filter (HPF)

In a constant-k HPF, the series arm is a capacitor ($Z_1 = 1/(j\\omega C)$) and the shunt arm is an inductor ($Z_2 = j\\omega L$).
Then $Z_1 Z_2 = L/C = R_0^2$. Cutoff frequency occurs at $\\frac{Z_1}{4Z_2} = -1$:

$$f_c = \\frac{1}{4\\pi \\sqrt{LC}}, \\qquad R_0 = \\sqrt{\\frac{L}{C}}$$

Design Formulas for Prototype HPF:

$$L = \\frac{R_0}{4\\pi f_c}, \\qquad C = \\frac{1}{4\\pi f_c R_0}$$

◆ 3. Limitations of Constant-k Filters

  • Slow Attenuation Transition: The attenuation $\\alpha$ rises very gradually above $f_c$, providing poor selectivity against adjacent unwanted signals.
  • Impedance Mismatch: $Z_{0T}$ drops to zero at $f_c$, while $Z_{0\\pi}$ approaches infinity at $f_c$. Terminating with a fixed resistor $R_0$ results in severe reflection loss near the cutoff frequency.

◆ 4. The m-Derived Filter Concept

To produce a rapid attenuation rise, Zobel designed a modified section whose series or shunt arm is resonated to create an infinite attenuation notch at a finite frequency $f_\\infty$ just beyond $f_c$, while keeping the characteristic impedance $Z_{0T}$ identical to the prototype section.

For an m-derived low-pass T-section ($0 < m < 1$):

  • Series arms: $Z_1' / 2 = m \\frac{Z_1}{2} = m \\frac{j\\omega L}{2}$.
  • Shunt arm: $Z_2' = \\frac{1 - m^2}{4m} Z_1 + m Z_2 = j\\omega \\left(\\frac{1 - m^2}{4m} L\\right) + \\frac{1}{j\\omega (m C)}$.

The shunt arm forms a series resonant circuit that shorts to ground at frequency $f_\\infty$:

$$\\omega_\\infty = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\left(\\frac{1-m^2}{4m} L\\right)(m C)}} = \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{LC} \\sqrt{1 - m^2}} = \\frac{\\omega_c}{\\sqrt{1 - m^2}}$$

Solving for the design parameter $m$:

$$m = \\sqrt{1 - \\left(\\frac{f_c}{f_\\infty}\\right)^2}, \\qquad (f_\\infty > f_c)$$

◆ 5. Terminating Half-Sections ($m = 0.6$)

To eliminate the impedance mismatch problem, an m-derived half-section (L-section) is placed at the input and output terminals. When terminated in a load $R_0$, the input impedance of an m-derived half-section with $m = 0.6$ is remarkably constant (within $\\pm 4\%$) over approximately $85\%$ of the passband!

◆ Worked Example: Complete Filter Design

Problem: Design a constant-k low-pass T-filter with $f_c = 2.5\,\\text{kHz}$ and $R_0 = 600\,\\Omega$. Find the required $m$ to place an infinite attenuation peak at $f_\\infty = 3.125\,\\text{kHz}$, and determine the shunt arm component values of the m-derived section.

Solution:
1. Prototype components:
$L = \\frac{R_0}{\\pi f_c} = \\frac{600}{\\pi \\times 2500} = 0.07639\,\\text{H} = 76.39\,\\text{mH}$.
Each series arm inductor of prototype T: $L/2 = 38.20\,\\text{mH}$.
$C = \\frac{1}{\\pi f_c R_0} = \\frac{1}{\\pi \\times 2500 \\times 600} = 0.2122\,\\mu\\text{F} = 212.2\,\\text{nF}$.
2. m parameter for $f_\\infty = 3.125\,\\text{kHz}$:
$m = \\sqrt{1 - (2500/3125)^2} = \\sqrt{1 - (0.8)^2} = \\sqrt{1 - 0.64} = \\sqrt{0.36} = 0.60$.
3. m-derived section components:
Series arms: $m(L/2) = 0.6 \\times 38.20\,\\text{mH} = 22.92\,\\text{mH}$ each.
Shunt inductor $L_2' = \\frac{1 - m^2}{4m} L = \\frac{1 - 0.36}{2.4} \\times 76.39\,\\text{mH} = 0.2667 \\times 76.39 = 20.37\,\\text{mH}$.
Shunt capacitor $C_2' = m C = 0.6 \\times 212.2\,\\text{nF} = 127.32\,\\text{nF}$.
Resonance check: $f_\\infty = \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\sqrt{20.37\\times 10^{-3} \\times 127.32\\times 10^{-9}}} = \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\times 5.0925\\times 10^{-5}} = 3125\,\\text{Hz} = 3.125\,\\text{kHz}$ ✓!

Common mistake: Calculating $m$ with an inverted ratio $f_\\infty / f_c$ for a low-pass filter, resulting in a negative square root. Remember $f_\\infty > f_c$ for low-pass, so $f_c / f_\\infty < 1$.
Placement trap: "Can an m-derived filter be used completely alone without a prototype section?" — While it has a sharp cutoff, beyond $f_\\infty$ its attenuation drops back down. Therefore, practical composite filters cascade a constant-k prototype (providing high attenuation at very high frequencies) with an m-derived section (providing sharp cutoff) and terminating half-sections ($m=0.6$, providing flat impedance matching).

◆ Interview Questions

"What is a composite filter and what are its three building blocks?" — A composite filter combines: (1) a constant-k prototype section for broad stopband attenuation; (2) one or more m-derived sections to generate steep cutoff transitions at specific interference frequencies $f_\\infty$; and (3) two m-derived terminating half-sections ($m=0.6$) at the input and output to ensure smooth impedance matching to the external load across the passband.

Digital circuits manipulate binary information using switching algebra formalized by George Boole and Claude Shannon. A complex logic specification can initially require dozens of gates, drawing excessive power and silicon area. By applying Boolean theorems and expressing functions in standard forms (SOP and POS), engineers algebraically simplify circuits to minimum gate counts with minimal propagation delay.

◆ 1. Boolean Postulates and Huntington's Axioms

For binary variables $A, B, C \\in \{0, 1\}$ and operations OR ($+$), AND ($\\cdot$), and NOT ($'$ or $\\bar{A}$):

Postulate / LawAND FormOR Form
Identity$A \\cdot 1 = A$$A + 0 = A$
Null Elements (Dominance)$A \\cdot 0 = 0$$A + 1 = 1$
Idempotent$A \\cdot A = A$$A + A = A$
Complementarity$A \\cdot \\bar{A} = 0$$A + \\bar{A} = 1$
Involution$\\overline{\\bar{A}} = A$
Commutative$A \\cdot B = B \\cdot A$$A + B = B + A$
Associative$(A \\cdot B) \\cdot C = A \\cdot (B \\cdot C)$$(A + B) + C = A + (B + C)$
Distributive$A + (B \\cdot C) = (A + B)(A + C)$$A \\cdot (B + C) = AB + AC$

Duality Principle: Any valid Boolean relation remains valid if AND and OR operators are interchanged, and $0$ and $1$ are interchanged, leaving variable complements unchanged.

◆ 2. De Morgan's Theorems

$$\\overline{A \\cdot B} = \\bar{A} + \\bar{B} \\qquad \\text{(NAND gate equivalent to Bubbled OR)}$$
$$\\overline{A + B} = \\bar{A} \\cdot \\bar{B} \\qquad \\text{(NOR gate equivalent to Bubbled AND)}$$

Generalized to $n$ variables: $\\overline{x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n} = \\bar{x}_1 + \\bar{x}_2 + \cdots + \\bar{x}_n$.

◆ 3. Canonical and Standard Forms

  • Minterm ($m_i$): A product term containing all $n$ literals in either true or complemented form, producing $1$ for exactly one input combination.
  • Maxterm ($M_i$): A sum term containing all $n$ literals in either true or complemented form, producing $0$ for exactly one input combination.
  • Complementary Relation: $M_i = \\overline{m_i}$.

Canonical Sum of Products (SOP): $F = \\sum m(1, 4, 7)$ — OR of minterms where $F = 1$.

Canonical Product of Sums (POS): $F = \prod M(0, 2, 3, 5, 6)$ — AND of maxterms where $F = 0$.

◆ Worked Example: Canonical Form Conversion

Problem: Express $F(A, B, C) = A + \\bar{B}C$ into canonical SOP form.

Solution:
Term 1: $A = A(B + \\bar{B})(C + \\bar{C}) = (AB + A\\bar{B})(C + \\bar{C}) = ABC + AB\\bar{C} + A\\bar{B}C + A\\bar{B}\\bar{C}$ ($m_7, m_6, m_5, m_4$).
Term 2: $\\bar{B}C = (A + \\bar{A})\\bar{B}C = A\\bar{B}C + \\bar{A}\\bar{B}C$ ($m_5, m_1$).
Combining and removing duplicates (idempotent law):
$F = \\bar{A}\\bar{B}C + A\\bar{B}\\bar{C} + A\\bar{B}C + AB\\bar{C} + ABC = m_1 + m_4 + m_5 + m_6 + m_7$.
Canonical SOP: $F(A, B, C) = \\sum m(1, 4, 5, 6, 7)$.
Canonical POS: $F(A, B, C) = \prod M(0, 2, 3)$ (the missing indices!). ✓

Common mistake: Forgetting that in minterms, uncomplemented variable represents $1$ and complemented represents $0$ (e.g., $A\\bar{B}C = 101_2 = m_5$), whereas in maxterms, uncomplemented represents $0$ and complemented represents $1$ (e.g., $A + \\bar{B} + C = 010_2 = M_2$).
Placement trap: "What is the dual of $A + \\bar{A}B = A + B$?" — Replace $+$ with $\\cdot$ and $\\cdot$ with $+$: $A( \\bar{A} + B) = AB$. Notice variable complements remain unchanged!

◆ Interview Questions

"Why is two-level AND-OR (SOP) logic preferred in high-speed hardware over multi-level logic?" — Two-level logic guarantees a constant propagation delay of exactly two gate delays (plus input inverters), maximizing switching speed and throughput compared to deep multi-level gate networks.

Algebraic simplification using Boolean theorems relies on pattern-matching intuition and easily misses optimal groupings. The Karnaugh Map (K-map), developed by Maurice Karnaugh in 1953, arranges truth-table minterms on an array where adjacent cells differ by exactly one binary variable (Gray code ordering). This converts complex Boolean algebraic minimization into visual geometric grouping of adjacent cells (powers of 2), guaranteeing a minimal two-level circuit.

◆ 1. Gray Code Cell Adjacency

In a 4-variable K-map ($A, B$ on rows; $C, D$ on columns), the row and column coordinates follow the 1-bit Gray code sequence: 00, 01, 11, 10.

  • Notice that $01 \to 11$ and $11 \to 10$ differ by only 1 bit.
  • Toroidal Wrapping: The top and bottom rows are adjacent ($00$ and $10$ differ by 1 bit). The leftmost and rightmost columns are adjacent ($00$ and $10$ differ by 1 bit). The four outer corners ($m_0, m_2, m_8, m_{10}$) form a valid group of 4!

◆ 2. Grouping Rules

  1. Groups must contain $2^k$ cells ($1, 2, 4, 8, 16$).
  2. Groups must be rectangular or square (no diagonals, L-shapes, or T-shapes).
  3. Every 1 must be covered by at least one group.
  4. Groups should be as large as possible to eliminate the maximum number of literals ($2^k$ cells in an $n$-variable map eliminates $k$ literals, leaving an $(n-k)$-literal product term).

◆ 3. Prime Implicants and Essential Prime Implicants

  • Implicant: Any product term that covers one or more 1s of the function.
  • Prime Implicant (PI): A rectangular group of $2^k$ 1s that cannot be combined with any other group to form a larger group.
  • Essential Prime Implicant (EPI): A Prime Implicant that contains at least one 1 that is NOT covered by any other prime implicant. All EPIs MUST appear in the minimal SOP expression!

◆ 4. Don't-Care Conditions ($d$)

Certain input combinations never occur in practical systems (e.g., states 10 to 15 in BCD circuits). These are denoted as don't-cares ($d$ or $X$). In K-map grouping, a don't-care is treated as a 1 if it helps enlarge a group of 1s, and treated as a 0 if it does not help.

◆ Worked Example: 4-Variable K-Map Minimization

Problem: Minimize $F(A,B,C,D) = \\sum m(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 14, 15) + d(1, 6)$.

Solution:
- Group 1 (Four corners + don't care $m_1$): Check corners: $m_0, m_2, m_8, m_{10}$ are all 1s. They wrap horizontally and vertically to form a quad: rows $00, 10$ eliminate $A$ (leaves $\\bar{B}$); columns $00, 10$ eliminate $C$ (leaves $\\bar{D}$). Term = $\\bar{B}\\bar{D}$.
- Group 2 (Quad of 1s and don't-cares at middle): cells $m_5, m_7$ (1s) and $m_1, d_6$ (don't care)? Look at column $01, 11$: $m_5, m_7$ combine with row $01$ ($A=0, B=1$) to form a quad with $m_1, d_6$ or combine $m_5, m_7, d_6, m_{14}$? Look at cells $m_5, m_7, m_{14}, m_{15}$: cells $m_5, m_7$ are in row 01; cells $m_{14}, m_{15}$ are in row 11. Columns 01 and 11: cells $m_5, m_7, m_{15}, d_{13}$? Cells $m_5(0101), m_7(0111), m_{13}(1101$ is 0$), m_{15}(1111)$. So $m_5, m_7$ form a pair with each other (gives $\\bar{A}BD$) or with $d_1$ (gives $\\bar{A}\\bar{C}D$)? If we include $d_1$: cells $m_1, m_5$ give $\\bar{A}\\bar{C}D$, and cells $m_5, m_7$ give $\\bar{A}BD$. Better: quad $m_1, m_5, m_7, d_3$? (d_3 is not given).
Let's look at $m_{14}, m_{15}$ (row 11): columns $11, 10$ give $AB C$. Together with $d_6(0110), m_7(0111)$ in row 01: cells $m_6(d), m_7(1), m_{14}(1), m_{15}(1)$ form a quad! Rows $01, 11$ eliminate $A$ (leaves $B$); columns $11, 10$ eliminate $D$ (leaves $C$). Term = $BC$.
- What covers $m_5(0101)$? Combine $m_5$ with $m_7$ and $d_1$ (cell 1) or $d_5$? Cell $m_5$ can combine with $m_7$ and $m_1(d), m_3(0)$? A pair of $m_5, m_7$ gives $\\bar{A}BD$. Alternatively $m_1(d), m_5$ gives $\\bar{A}\\bar{C}D$.
Minimal expression: $F = \\bar{B}\\bar{D} + BC + \\bar{A}BD$. ✓

Common mistake: Grouping don't-cares with each other when they do not cover any true 1s. Don't-cares should NEVER be grouped together in isolation — they are only used to expand groups containing at least one real 1.
Placement trap: "What causes a static-1 hazard in a combinational circuit derived from a minimal K-map?" — Adjacent 1-cells covered by different prime implicants without an overlapping consensus term. As inputs transition between the groups, gate delay differences can cause a brief spurious 0 glitch.

◆ Interview Questions

"How do you eliminate a static hazard in K-map design?" — Add an extra redundant prime implicant that bridges across the adjacent boundary of the two original groups. While algebraically redundant, this consensus term ensures the output remains firmly at 1 during the transition.

Arithmetic operations form the foundational core of modern computing, executed billions of times per second inside microprocessors, GPUs, and DSP chips. Addition and subtraction are the primary primitives — multiplication is repeated addition, and division is repeated subtraction. Designing high-speed, glitch-free adders and subtractors is essential for high-performance ALU architectures.

◆ 1. Half Adder (HA)

Adds two single binary bits $A$ and $B$, generating Sum ($S$) and Carry ($C$):

$$S = A \oplus B = A\\bar{B} + \\bar{A}B, \\qquad C = A \\cdot B$$
  • Truth Table: $(0,0)\to(0,0); (0,1)\to(1,0); (1,0)\to(1,0); (1,1)\to(0,1)$.
  • NAND-only Implementation: Requires exactly 5 two-input NAND gates.
  • NOR-only Implementation: Requires exactly 5 two-input NOR gates.

◆ 2. Full Adder (FA)

Adds two single binary bits $A$ and $B$ along with an incoming carry from the previous stage $C_{in}$:

$$S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}$$
$$C_{out} = AB + BC_{in} + AC_{in} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)$$

Implementation using Two Half Adders:

  • HA 1: $S_1 = A \oplus B$, $C_1 = AB$.
  • HA 2: $S = S_1 \oplus C_{in} = (A \oplus B) \oplus C_{in}$, $C_2 = S_1 \\cdot C_{in} = (A \oplus B)C_{in}$.
  • Final Carry: $C_{out} = C_1 + C_2 = AB + (A \oplus B)C_{in}$. (Note: $C_1$ and $C_2$ can never be 1 simultaneously, so an OR gate or XOR gate can combine them).
  • Requires: 2 Half Adders + 1 OR gate (or 9 NAND gates).

◆ 3. Half Subtractor (HS)

Subtracts bit $B$ from bit $A$, generating Difference ($D$) and Borrow ($B_{out}$):

$$D = A \oplus B, \\qquad B_{out} = \\bar{A} \\cdot B$$

Notice that Difference $D$ is identical to the Half Adder Sum $S$!

◆ 4. Full Subtractor (FS)

Computes $A - B - B_{in}$:

$$D = A \oplus B \oplus B_{in}$$
$$B_{out} = \\bar{A}B + \\bar{A}B_{in} + BB_{in} = \\bar{A}B + B_{in}\\overline{(A \oplus B)}$$

Can be constructed using 2 Half Subtractors + 1 OR gate.

◆ Worked Example: Gate Delay Analysis

Problem: In a Full Adder implemented with 2 Half Adders and an OR gate, each XOR gate has a propagation delay of $12\,\\text{ns}$ and each AND/OR gate has a delay of $8\,\\text{ns}$. Calculate the propagation delay to produce the Sum $S$ and the Carry $C_{out}$.

Solution:
- Sum path: $S = (A \oplus B) \oplus C_{in}$ → passes through two consecutive XOR gates.
$t_{delay}(S) = 12\,\\text{ns} + 12\,\\text{ns} = 24\,\\text{ns}.
- Carry path: $C_2 = (A \oplus B)C_{in}$ takes $12\,\\text{ns} (\\text{XOR}) + 8\,\\text{ns} (\\text{AND}) = 20\,\\text{ns}$.
Then $C_{out} = C_1 + C_2$ passes through the OR gate: $20\,\\text{ns} + 8\,\\text{ns} (\\text{OR}) = 28\,\\text{ns}.
(Path through $C_1 = AB$ is only $8\,\\text{ns} + 8\,\\text{ns} = 16\,\\text{ns}$, so the $C_2$ path is the critical path).
Critical delay of the Full Adder: $28\,\\text{ns}$. ✓

Common mistake: Assuming Borrow in a subtractor is $A\\bar{B}$. The borrow is $\\bar{A}B$ because a borrow is needed only when subtracting a larger number ($B=1$) from a smaller number ($A=0$).
Placement trap: "How many NAND gates are required to implement a Full Adder?" — Exactly 9 two-input NAND gates.

◆ Interview Questions

"How can an adder be converted into a subtractor without altering the adder hardware?" — By using 2's complement arithmetic: invert the subtrahend bits (using XOR gates with control signal $M=1$) and inject $C_{in} = 1$ into the least significant bit position ($A - B = A + \\bar{B} + 1$).

When cascading single-bit Full Adders into an $n$-bit Ripple Carry Adder (RCA), the carry bit must sequentially ripple through every stage from LSB to MSB before the final sum bits become valid. For a 32-bit or 64-bit word, this creates an intolerable latency bottleneck. The Carry Lookahead Adder (CLA) solves this fundamental problem by computing all carries simultaneously in parallel using two-level logic, reducing addition delay from $O(n)$ to $O(1)$.

◆ 1. Ripple Carry Adder (RCA) Bottleneck

A 4-bit parallel adder cascades 4 Full Adders where $C_{out}$ of stage $i$ connects to $C_{in}$ of stage $i+1$.

  • For $n$ bits, the total worst-case delay is:
    $$t_{RCA} = t_{HA} + (n - 1) t_{carry} + t_{sum}$$
  • For a 64-bit RCA with $t_{gate} = 1\,\\text{ns}$, addition takes over $130\,\\text{ns}$, capping clock frequency at < 8 MHz!

◆ 2. 4-Bit Parallel Adder/Subtractor (Controlled Inversion)

By connecting one input of an XOR gate to each data bit $B_i$ and the other input to a mode control line $M$:

  • When $M = 0$ (Addition): $B_i \oplus 0 = B_i$, and $C_{in} = M = 0$. Circuit computes $A + B + 0 = A + B$.
  • When $M = 1$ (Subtraction): $B_i \oplus 1 = \\bar{B}_i$ (1's complement), and $C_{in} = M = 1$. Circuit computes $A + \\bar{B} + 1 = A - B$ (2's complement addition!).
  • An overflow flag $V$ is generated by: $V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1}$. For signed numbers, $V = 1$ indicates arithmetic overflow.

◆ 3. Carry Lookahead Principle: Generate ($G$) and Propagate ($P$)

For stage $i$:

$$G_i = A_i B_i \\qquad \\text{(Carry Generate — stage produces carry regardless of incoming carry)}$$
$$P_i = A_i \oplus B_i \\qquad \\text{(Carry Propagate — stage propagates incoming carry to output)}$$

The carry out of stage $i$ is: $C_{i+1} = G_i + P_i C_i$.

Expanding recursively for a 4-bit block:

$$C_1 = G_0 + P_0 C_0$$
$$C_2 = G_1 + P_1 C_1 = G_1 + P_1 G_0 + P_1 P_0 C_0$$
$$C_3 = G_2 + P_2 G_1 + P_2 P_1 G_0 + P_2 P_1 P_0 C_0$$
$$C_4 = G_3 + P_3 G_2 + P_3 P_2 G_1 + P_3 P_2 P_1 G_0 + P_3 P_2 P_1 P_0 C_0$$

Critical Insight: Every carry $C_1, C_2, C_3, C_4$ depends only on the original inputs $A, B$ and initial carry $C_0$! All carries are computed simultaneously through just 2 gate delays (AND level then OR level), completely bypassing the serial ripple chain!

◆ Worked Example: Delay Comparison

Problem: Compare the worst-case carry computation delay between a 16-bit Ripple Carry Adder and a 16-bit Carry Lookahead Adder (built of four 4-bit CLA blocks with a lookahead carry generator), assuming all logic gates have a propagation delay of $2\,\\text{ns}$ and XOR gates have $3\,\\text{ns}$.

Solution:
1. 16-bit Ripple Carry Adder:
Carry from each stage takes 2 gate delays ($4\,\\text{ns}$).
Total carry propagation through 16 stages: $16 \\times 4\,\\text{ns} = 64\,\\text{ns}.
2. 16-bit Hierarchical CLA:
- Step 1: All $P_i, G_i$ generated in parallel: $3\,\\text{ns}$ (XOR delay).
- Step 2: Block carry lookahead generator computes block carries in 2 gate levels: $2 \\times 2 = 4\,\\text{ns}$.
- Step 3: Local carries within each block computed in 2 gate levels: $2 \\times 2 = 4\,\\text{ns}$.
- Step 4: Final sum bits $S_i = P_i \oplus C_i$: $3\,\\text{ns}$.
Total delay of 16-bit CLA: $3 + 4 + 4 + 3 = 14\,\\text{ns}.
Speedup: $\\frac{64\,\\text{ns}}{14\,\\text{ns}} \\approx 4.57\\times$ faster! ✓

Common mistake: Using $P_i = A_i + B_i$ instead of $A_i \oplus B_i$ when computing the sum. While $A_i + B_i$ can mathematically propagate carry, $S_i = P_i \oplus C_i$ requires $P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$ to yield the correct sum bit.
Placement trap: "Why aren't single-block CLAs built for 32 or 64 bits directly?" — Because the gate fan-in (number of inputs per gate) required for $C_{32}$ or $C_{64}$ would exceed physical limits (requiring 33 to 65 input AND/OR gates). Instead, hierarchical 4-bit blocks with Lookahead Carry Units (e.g., 74182) are cascaded.

◆ Interview Questions

"What is the condition for signed overflow when adding two numbers in an $n$-bit parallel adder?" — Signed overflow occurs when the carry into the sign bit ($C_{n-1}$) does not equal the carry out of the sign bit ($C_n$), mathematically given by $V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1} = 1$.

Digital systems constantly compare numeric values — branch conditions in CPUs ($A > B$, $A = B$), limit testing in control systems, and priority scheduling. Furthermore, data transmitted across noisy physical channels (buses, wireless links, memory interfaces) is susceptible to bit flips. Parity circuits provide instantaneous hardware error detection with minimal gate overhead.

◆ 1. Magnitude Comparators

A magnitude comparator compares two $n$-bit binary numbers $A$ and $B$, generating three mutually exclusive outputs: $A > B$, $A = B$, and $A < B$.

  • 1-Bit Comparator:
    $A = B$: $E = A \odot B = AB + \\bar{A}\\bar{B}$ (XNOR / Equivalence gate).
    $A > B$: $G = A\\bar{B}$.
    $A < B$: $L = \\bar{A}B$.
  • 2-Bit Magnitude Comparator:
    $A = B$: $(A_1 \odot B_1) \\cdot (A_0 \odot B_0)$.
    $A > B$: $A_1 \\bar{B}_1 + (A_1 \odot B_1) A_0 \\bar{B}_0$. (MSBs compared first; if equal, LSBs decide!).
    $A < B$: $\\bar{A}_1 B_1 + (A_1 \odot B_1) \\bar{A}_0 B_0$.
  • Standard MSI Comparator: 74LS85 (4-Bit): Has cascading inputs ($I_{A>B}, I_{A=B}, I_{AB}, I_{A

◆ 2. Parity Generators and Checkers

Parity is an error-detection code where an extra bit (parity bit $P$) is appended to data so that the total count of 1s is always even (Even Parity) or always odd (Odd Parity).

  • Even Parity Generator: Produces $P = 1$ when the data word contains an odd number of 1s (making total 1s even):
    $$P_{\\text{even}} = A \oplus B \oplus C \oplus D$$
  • Odd Parity Generator:
    $$P_{\\text{odd}} = \\overline{A \oplus B \oplus C \oplus D} = (A \oplus B \oplus C \oplus D)'$$
  • Parity Checker (Receiver Side): Evaluates the received word $A, B, C, D$ along with received parity bit $P$.
    $$\\text{Error (Even Parity)} = A \oplus B \oplus C \oplus D \oplus P$$
    If $\\text{Error} = 0$, no single-bit error occurred. If $\\text{Error} = 1$, a transmission error is flagged!
  • Limitation: Parity detects all single-bit errors (and any odd number of bit errors), but CANNOT detect an even number of bit flips (e.g. 2 bits flipped).

◆ Worked Example: Parity Generation & Checking

Problem: A 4-bit data word $D = 1011_2$ is transmitted using an Even Parity scheme. (a) Determine the parity bit $P$. (b) If noise flips the third bit during transmission so the receiver reads $1001_2$ with the received $P$, show how the parity checker flags the error.

Solution:
(a) Data bits: $A=1, B=0, C=1, D=1$. Count of 1s = 3 (odd).
Even parity generator: $P = 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 1 \oplus 1 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1.
Transmitted 5-bit frame: $10111_2$ (total 1s = 4, which is even ✓).
(b) Received frame: $10011_2$ ($A=1, B=0, C=0, D=1, P=1$).
Checker evaluates parity sum: $C_{err} = 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1 \oplus 1 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1.
Because $C_{err} = 1$, the parity checker flags a transmission error! ✓

Common mistake: Assuming an XNOR gate is used for even parity. The XOR gate is an odd-detector (outputs 1 for odd number of 1s). To make the total number of 1s even, we need an extra 1 whenever the data has an odd number of 1s — so an XOR gate IS the even parity generator!
Placement trap: "If a transmission link has a 2-bit error, will a parity checker detect it?" — No. Parity checks only detect an odd number of errors ($1, 3, 5\dots$). Two bit flips preserve the original parity.

◆ Interview Questions

"How does a magnitude comparator cascade when comparing wide words (e.g. 16 bits)?" — The most significant 4-bit slice compares first. If the MSB slice finds $A > B$ or $A < B$, its output immediately determines the overall result. Only when the MSB slice finds equality ($A = B$) does it enable the next lower slice via cascading inputs ($I_{A=B}$), rippling down to the LSB.

A Multiplexer (MUX) is a digital rotary switch that routes one of several input lines to a single output line based on binary select inputs. MUXes are universal logic modules — any arbitrary $n$-variable Boolean function can be implemented using an $n-1$ select-line MUX with no external gates. The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) combines multiplexer data-steering with adder/subtractor logic to perform all fundamental arithmetic and bitwise computations inside every computer processor.

◆ 1. Multiplexers (Data Selectors)

An $2^n$-to-1 MUX has $2^n$ data inputs ($I_0..I_{2^n-1}$), $n$ select lines ($S_{n-1}..S_0$), an enable line ($E$), and a single output $Y$:

$$4\\text{-to-}1\\text{ MUX: } Y = \\bar{S}_1\\bar{S}_0 I_0 + \\bar{S}_1 S_0 I_1 + S_1\\bar{S}_0 I_2 + S_1 S_0 I_3$$

Universal Logic Synthesis using MUX:

To implement an $n$-variable function $F(A, B, C)$ using a $2^{n-1}$-to-1 MUX (e.g. 4-to-1 MUX for 3 variables):

  1. Connect $n-1$ variables (e.g., $A, B$) to select lines $S_1, S_0$.
  2. For each select combination, evaluate $F$ in terms of the remaining variable $C$: each data input $I_k$ will be either $0, 1, C,$ or $\\bar{C}$!

◆ 2. Demultiplexers (DEMUX)

A Demultiplexer performs the reverse operation: it routes a single data input $D_{in}$ to one of $2^n$ output lines based on $n$ select lines.

Decoder vs Demultiplexer: A decoder with an enable line is functionally identical to a demultiplexer! The enable input of the decoder acts as the data input $D_{in}$ of the demultiplexer.

◆ 3. Architecture of Arithmetic Logic Units (ALUs)

A typical 4-bit ALU slice (e.g. 74LS181) can perform 16 arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, increment, decrement) and 16 logic operations (AND, OR, XOR, NOT, NAND):

  • Inputs: Operands $A[3:0], B[3:0]$, Function select $S[3:0]$, Mode control $M$, Carry in $C_n$.
  • Mode Control $M$:
    • $M = 1$ (Logic Mode): All internal carries are disabled. The ALU performs bitwise operations independently on each bit without carry propagation.
    • $M = 0$ (Arithmetic Mode): Carries are enabled with lookahead logic. Operations take carry-in $C_n$ into account (e.g. $A + B$, $A - B - 1$, $A + A$).
  • Status Flags: Zero flag ($Z=1$ when output is $0000$), Carry flag ($C_{out}$), Sign flag (MSB of result), and Overflow flag ($V$).

◆ Worked Example: Function Implementation using MUX

Problem: Implement $F(A, B, C) = \\sum m(1, 2, 4, 7)$ using a 4-to-1 MUX with $A$ and $B$ connected to select lines $S_1$ and $S_0$.

Solution:
Construct implementation table with $S_1 = A, S_0 = B$ and input variable $C$:
- When $AB = 00$ (row $m_0, m_1$): $F(0,0,0) = 0, F(0,0,1) = 1 \implies Y = C$. Set $I_0 = C$.
- When $AB = 01$ (row $m_2, m_3$): $F(0,1,0) = 1, F(0,1,1) = 0 \implies Y = \\bar{C}$. Set $I_1 = \\bar{C}$.
- When $AB = 10$ (row $m_4, m_5$): $F(1,0,0) = 1, F(1,0,1) = 0 \implies Y = \\bar{C}$. Set $I_2 = \\bar{C}$.
- When $AB = 11$ (row $m_6, m_7$): $F(1,1,0) = 0, F(1,1,1) = 1 \implies Y = C$. Set $I_3 = C$.
Result: Connect $I_0 = C, I_1 = \\bar{C}, I_2 = \\bar{C}, I_3 = C$ to the 4-to-1 MUX inputs. The function is realized with zero additional gates (beyond an inverter for $\\bar{C}$)! ✓

Common mistake: Confusing MUX and DEMUX definitions. A MUX is $2^n$-to-1 (many inputs to one output); a DEMUX is 1-to-$2^n$ (one input to many outputs).
Placement trap: "How many 2-to-1 MUXes are needed to build an 8-to-1 MUX?" — Exactly 7 MUXes (4 in the first level, 2 in the second, and 1 in the third). In general, a $2^n$-to-1 MUX requires $2^n - 1$ two-to-one MUX units.

◆ Interview Questions

"What is the difference between arithmetic mode and logic mode in the 74181 ALU?" — In logic mode ($M = 1$), carry propagation across bit positions is completely suppressed by disabling internal carry gates, allowing bitwise logical operations (AND, OR, XOR) without inter-bit interference. In arithmetic mode ($M = 0$), internal carry lookahead logic is activated, allowing multi-bit addition and subtraction.

Modern microprocessors containing billions of transistors cannot be designed using manual schematic drafting. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs) like Verilog allow engineers to describe, simulate, synthesize, and verify complex digital circuits programmatically. Mastering Verilog's three levels of abstraction (Gate-Level, Dataflow, Behavioral) is the core technical skill required for ASIC and FPGA engineering careers.

◆ 1. Verilog Language Elements

  • Module: Fundamental building block enclosed between module name(port_list); and endmodule.
  • Port Types: input, output, inout.
  • Data Types:
    • wire: Represents a physical electrical connection; driven continuously by gates or assign statements.
    • reg: Represents a procedural data storage variable; holds values between assignments in always or initial blocks (does NOT always synthesize to a physical flip-flop!).
  • Logic Values (4-state): 0 (logic low), 1 (logic high), z (high impedance / floating), x (unknown / contention).
  • Number Literals: <size>'<base><value> — e.g. 4'b1010 (binary), 8'hFF (hexadecimal), 16'd100 (decimal).

◆ 2. Gate-Level Modeling

Uses built-in primitives: and, or, nand, nor, xor, xnor, not.

Syntax: primitive_name instance_id (output, input1, input2, ...);

Example: XOR gate using only NAND gates:

module xor_from_nand(input A, B, output Y);
  wire w1, w2, w3;
  nand n1(w1, A, B);
  nand n2(w2, A, w1);
  nand n3(w3, w1, B);
  nand n4(Y, w2, w3);
endmodule

◆ 3. Dataflow Modeling

Uses continuous assignment with the assign keyword and Boolean/arithmetic operators. Updates instantly whenever any operand on the right-hand side changes.

// 1-Bit Full Adder in Dataflow
module full_adder_dataflow(input A, B, Cin, output S, Cout);
  assign S = A ^ B ^ Cin;
  assign Cout = (A & B) | (Cin & (A ^ B));
endmodule

// 4:1 Multiplexer in Dataflow using ternary operator
module mux4to1(input [3:0] I, input [1:0] S, output Y);
  assign Y = (S == 2'b00) ? I[0] :
             (S == 2'b01) ? I[1] :
             (S == 2'b10) ? I[2] : I[3];
endmodule

◆ 4. Behavioral Modeling

Uses procedural blocks (always, initial) with sequential statements (if-else, case). Variables assigned inside must be of type reg.

// 3-to-8 Decoder Behavioral
module decoder3to8(input [2:0] in, input enable, output reg [7:0] out);
  always @(*) begin
    if (!enable)
      out = 8'b00000000;
    else begin
      out = 8'b00000000;
      out[in] = 1'b1;
    end
  end
endmodule

Combinational Rule: In combinational always @(*) blocks, ALWAYS use blocking assignments (=) and ensure all branches of if-else or case assign every output variable to prevent inferring unintended transparent latches!

◆ 5. Verilog Testbench

A module with no inputs/outputs that instantiates the Device Under Test (DUT) and drives stimulus using initial blocks, delays (#10), and monitoring statements ($display, $monitor, $finish).

Common mistake: Using a wire data type on the left-hand side of an assignment inside an always block. Any variable assigned inside an always block MUST be declared as reg.
Placement trap: "What causes an unwanted latch in combinational Verilog?" — Missing an else branch in an if statement, or omitting cases without a default clause in a case statement. The synthesis tool infers a memory latch to hold the previous value!

◆ Interview Questions

"What is the difference between blocking (=) and non-blocking (<=) assignments in Verilog?" — Blocking assignments (=) execute sequentially in order, blocking execution of subsequent statements until the current assignment completes; they must be used for combinational logic. Non-blocking assignments (<=) evaluate right-hand sides simultaneously at the current time step and schedule updates at the end of the time step without blocking; they MUST be used for sequential logic (registers/flip-flops) to prevent simulation race conditions.

Combinational circuits produce outputs that depend solely on current inputs. Sequential circuits, by contrast, possess memory — their outputs depend on both current inputs and the stored history of past operations. Flip-flops are the fundamental 1-bit memory building blocks of all registers, cache memories, microprocessors, and state machines.

◆ 1. Latches vs. Edge-Triggered Flip-Flops

  • Latch: Level-sensitive bistable element. Changes output continuously as long as the enable/clock input is held HIGH (transparent). Highly vulnerable to glitches and race conditions.
  • Flip-Flop: Edge-triggered bistable element. Samples inputs and updates output strictly on the transitioning edge (rising 0→1 or falling 1→0) of the clock pulse.
  • SR Latch (Active-High NOR): Inputs $S$ (Set), $R$ (Reset).
    • $S=0, R=0$: No change ($Q_{next} = Q$).
    • $S=0, R=1$: Reset ($Q_{next} = 0$).
    • $S=1, R=0$: Set ($Q_{next} = 1$).
    • $S=1, R=1$: Forbidden / Invalid state (both $Q$ and $\\bar{Q}$ forced to 0; race condition upon removal).

◆ 2. JK, D, and T Flip-Flops

Flip-FlopInputsCharacteristic EquationExcitation Rule ($Q \to Q_{next}$)
SR$S, R$ ($SR=0$)$Q_{next} = S + R'Q$$0\to0: S=0,R=X$; $0\to1: S=1,R=0$; $1\to0: S=0,R=1$; $1\to1: S=X,R=0$
JK$J, K$$Q_{next} = JQ' + K'Q$$0\to0: J=0,K=X$; $0\to1: J=1,K=X$; $1\to0: J=X,K=1$; $1\to1: J=X,K=0$
D$D$ (Data)$Q_{next} = D$$0\to0: D=0$; $0\to1: D=1$; $1\to0: D=0$; $1\to1: D=1$
T$T$ (Toggle)$Q_{next} = T \oplus Q$$0\to0: T=0$; $0\to1: T=1$; $1\to0: T=1$; $1\to1: T=0$

◆ 3. The Race-Around Condition & Master-Slave JK Flip-Flop

In a level-triggered JK flip-flop with $J=1, K=1$, if the clock pulse width $t_p$ is greater than the propagation delay of the flip-flop $\\Delta t$ ($t_p > \\Delta t$), the output will toggle repeatedly (oscillate between 0 and 1) during the single clock pulse, leaving an unpredictable state at the falling edge. This is the race-around condition.

  • Conditions for Race-Around: (1) Level-triggered JK flip-flop; (2) $J = 1, K = 1$; (3) Pulse duration $t_p > \\Delta t$.
  • Cure 1: Master-Slave JK Flip-Flop: Consists of two flip-flops cascaded in series. The Master is enabled on the clock HIGH level ($CLK=1$); the Slave is enabled on the inverted clock ($CLK=0$). Data enters the master during HIGH and transfers to the slave during the falling edge. The complete cycle isolates input from output, completely eliminating race-around!
  • Cure 2: Edge-triggering: Using RC differentiator circuits or internal cross-coupled gate propagation delays to respond only within a sub-nanosecond clock edge window.

◆ 4. Systematic Flip-Flop Conversion Methodology

  1. Identify Available Flip-Flop (inputs known) and Target Flip-Flop (inputs given).
  2. Construct a unified Conversion Table listing Target Inputs, Present State $Q$, Next State $Q_{next}$, and the required Available Flip-Flop inputs (from its Excitation Table).
  3. Plot Karnaugh maps for each available input treating Target Inputs and $Q$ as variables.
  4. Synthesize minimal logic expressions and draw the inter-gate conversion circuit.

◆ Worked Example: Converting JK Flip-Flop to D Flip-Flop

Problem: Design a circuit to convert an available JK flip-flop into a D flip-flop.

Solution:
Target is D ($Q_{next} = D$). Available is JK ($J, K$).
Conversion table:
• $D=0, Q=0 \implies Q_{next}=0 \implies J=0, K=X$
• $D=0, Q=1 \implies Q_{next}=0 \implies J=X, K=1$
• $D=1, Q=0 \implies Q_{next}=1 \implies J=1, K=X$
• $D=1, Q=1 \implies Q_{next}=1 \implies J=X, K=0$
K-map for $J$: $J(D, Q) = D$ (since $J(0,0)=0, J(0,1)=X, J(1,0)=1, J(1,1)=X$).
K-map for $K$: $K(D, Q) = \\bar{D}$ (since $K(0,0)=X, K(0,1)=1, K(1,0)=X, K(1,1)=0$).
Conclusion: Connect $D$ directly to $J$, and connect $\\bar{D}$ (via an inverter) to $K$ ($J = D$, $K = D'$). ✓

Common mistake: Confusing the Characteristic Table with the Excitation Table. The Characteristic Table finds $Q_{next}$ from given inputs; the Excitation Table determines the required inputs to force a given state transition ($Q \to Q_{next}$). Counter and conversion designs ALWAYS use the Excitation Table!
Placement trap: "Can a D flip-flop suffer from the race-around condition?" — No. Race-around occurs strictly when an output feeds back to toggle the input while the clock is transparent (as in $J=1, K=1$ or $T=1$). A D flip-flop simply transfers $D$ to $Q$, with no toggling feedback.

◆ Interview Questions

"What is setup time and hold time in a flip-flop?" — Setup time ($t_{su}$) is the minimum duration the data input must remain stable BEFORE the triggering clock edge. Hold time ($t_h$) is the minimum duration the data input must remain stable AFTER the triggering clock edge. Violating either causes the flip-flop to enter an unpredictable metastable state.

Shift registers are the primary hardware mechanism for data format transformation — converting high-speed parallel computer words into serial bit streams for USB, Ethernet, and PCIe transmission, and converting them back at the receiver. Ring and Johnson counters generate multiphase non-overlapping clock pulses for brushless motor commutation and pipeline scheduling.

◆ 1. The Four Basic Shift Register Architectures

TypeAcronymInput MethodOutput MethodClock Pulses for $n$ Bits
Serial-In Serial-OutSISO1 bit per clock (serial line)1 bit per clock after $n$ shifts$n$ to load, $n-1$ to read out ($2n-1$ total)
Serial-In Parallel-OutSIPO1 bit per clock (serial line)All $n$ bits simultaneously$n$ clock pulses to load data
Parallel-In Serial-OutPISOAll $n$ bits loaded at once ($\\text{Shift}/\\overline{\\text{Load}}=0$)1 bit per clock via serial out1 pulse to load + $(n-1)$ pulses to read
Parallel-In Parallel-OutPIPOAll $n$ bits loaded at onceAll $n$ bits available immediately1 clock pulse (acts as a buffer register)

◆ 2. Universal Shift Register (e.g., 74LS194)

Can perform all 4 modes of operation as well as bidirectional shifting (Left/Right) controlled by two mode select lines ($S_1, S_0$):

  • $S_1 S_0 = 00$: Hold (no change; outputs recirculate).
  • $S_1 S_0 = 01$: Shift-Right (towards LSB; $Q_3 \to Q_2 \to Q_1 \to Q_0$).
  • $S_1 S_0 = 10$: Shift-Left (towards MSB; $Q_0 \to Q_1 \to Q_2 \to Q_3$).
  • $S_1 S_0 = 11$: Parallel Load (accepts 4 parallel data inputs $D_3..D_0$).

◆ 3. Ring Counter vs. Johnson (Twisted-Ring) Counter

  • Ring Counter: Formed by connecting the serial output $Q_0$ of the last stage back to the serial input $D_{n-1}$ of the first stage.
    • Starts with a circulating single 1: e.g. $1000 \to 0100 \to 0010 \to 0001 \to 1000$.
    • Number of distinct states: $M = n$ (for $n$ flip-flops).
    • Unused states: $2^n - n$ states!
    • Advantage: Decoded outputs require no external decoding gates (each flip-flop output represents a unique phase).
  • Johnson Counter (Moebius / Twisted Ring): Formed by connecting the inverted serial output $\\bar{Q}_0$ of the last stage back to the serial input $D_{n-1}$ of the first stage.
    • Sequence for 4 bits: $0000 \to 1000 \to 1100 \to 1110 \to 1111 \to 0111 \to 0011 \to 0001 \to 0000$.
    • Number of distinct states: $M = 2n$ (twice that of a ring counter!).
    • Unused states: $2^n - 2n$.
    • Decoding: Each state can be decoded using a simple 2-input AND gate (e.g., state $0000$ decoded by $\\bar{Q}_3 \\bar{Q}_0$).

◆ Worked Example: Johnson Counter Decoding & Frequency Division

Problem: A 5-stage Johnson counter is clocked at $f_{in} = 20\,\\text{MHz}$. (a) Determine the output frequency at any single flip-flop output. (b) Find the total number of decoded states. (c) Write the Boolean decoding expression for the state $S = 11100_2$ ($Q_4 Q_3 Q_2 Q_1 Q_0$).

Solution:
(a) A Johnson counter with $n$ stages has modulus $M = 2n = 2 \\times 5 = 10$.
Any single flip-flop output toggles at: $$f_{out} = \\frac{f_{in}}{2n} = \\frac{20\,\\text{MHz}}{10} = 2\,\\text{MHz}$$ with a 50% duty cycle! ✓
(b) Decoded states = $2n = 10$ states. (Unused states = $2^5 - 10 = 32 - 10 = 22$).
(c) In state $11100_2$: $Q_4=1, Q_3=1, Q_2=1, Q_1=0, Q_0=0$. Notice the boundary where bits change: $Q_2=1$ and $Q_1=0$.
In a Johnson counter, each state is uniquely identified by the position of the 1→0 or 0→1 transition! Here, the transition occurs between stages 2 and 1: $Y = Q_2 \\cdot \\bar{Q}_1$. ✓

Common mistake: Assuming a Ring counter has $2^n$ states. A Ring counter has only $n$ states because only one '1' circulates. A 4-bit Ring counter has 4 states; a 4-bit Johnson counter has 8 states.
Placement trap: "If power-up initializes a 4-bit Johnson counter to $0101_2$, what will happen?" — $0101_2$ is an unused state! The inverted feedback will produce: $0101 \to 0010 \to 1001 \to 0100 \to 1010 \dots$ cycling forever in a parasitic sub-loop! An initialization/reset circuit is required to force it into $0000$.

◆ Interview Questions

"Why is a Johnson counter preferred over a binary counter for multiphase clock generation?" — (1) Only one bit changes per clock transition (Gray-code property), completely preventing decoding glitches/spikes. (2) Each decoded state requires only a simple 2-input gate regardless of word length, whereas an $n$-bit binary counter requires $n$-input decoding gates.

Digital hardware synthesis tools strictly require RTL (Register-Transfer Level) code that cleanly distinguishes between combinational clouds and clocked memory elements. Writing synthesizable sequential Verilog with correct sensitivity lists, reset methodologies (synchronous vs asynchronous), and non-blocking assignments is the foundation of production ASIC/SoC design.

◆ 1. The Sequential Procedural Block

Sequential logic in Verilog is modeled using an edge-sensitive always block:

always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin ... end
  • Golden Rule: Inside sequential always @(posedge clk) blocks, ALWAYS use Non-Blocking Assignments (<=). Never use blocking (=) assignments for flip-flops!
  • Why Non-Blocking? In hardware, all flip-flops update simultaneously on the clock edge. Non-blocking assignments evaluate all right-hand sides before updating left-hand sides at the end of the time step, preventing race conditions between cascaded stages in simulation.

◆ 2. Asynchronous vs. Synchronous Reset

  • Asynchronous Reset: Reset takes effect immediately, regardless of the clock: 
    // D Flip-Flop with Active-High Asynchronous Reset
always @(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin
  if (rst)
    q <= 1'b0;
  else
    q <= d;
end
  • Synchronous Reset: Reset is evaluated only on the rising clock edge: 
    // D Flip-Flop with Active-High Synchronous Reset
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst)
    q <= 1'b0;
  else
    q <= d;
end
    Notice: rst is NOT included in the sensitivity list!

◆ 3. Synthesizable Verilog Counters

4-Bit Synchronous Binary Up-Counter with Synchronous Clear & Load:

module counter_4bit(
  input clk,
  input rst_n,       // Active-low asynchronous reset
  input clr,         // Synchronous clear
  input load,        // Parallel load enable
  input en,          // Count enable
  input [3:0] d_in,  // Parallel data
  output reg [3:0] count
);
  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
      count <= 4'b0000;
    else if (clr)
      count <= 4'b0000;
    else if (load)
      count <= d_in;
    else if (en)
      count <= count + 1'b1;
  end
endmodule

◆ 4. Shift Register Modeling

A 4-bit Serial-In Parallel-Out (SIPO) shift register is modeled cleanly using concatenation:

module sipo_reg(
  input clk, rst, sin,
  output reg [3:0] q
);
  always @(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin
    if (rst)
      q <= 4'b0000;
    else
      q <= {q[2:0], sin}; // Left-shift: shifts bits left and appends sin to LSB
  end
endmodule
Common mistake: Mixing blocking (=) and non-blocking (<=) assignments within the same sequential always block. This leads to unpredictable simulation-synthesis mismatches.
Placement trap: "What happens if you omit the reset signal from the sensitivity list in an intended asynchronous reset block?" — The synthesis tool will infer a SYNCHRONOUS reset instead, because the block only triggers on the clock edge!

◆ Interview Questions

"Why is asynchronous reset preferred in some designs while synchronous reset is favored in FPGA designs?" — Asynchronous reset guarantees that the chip resets immediately even if the clock tree has not started or is hung, and it saves datapath logic. However, releasing an asynchronous reset can cause metastability if deasserted too close to the clock edge (reset recovery/removal violation). Modern FPGAs prefer synchronous resets because dedicated flip-flop control sets support synchronous resets directly with higher clock frequencies.

All digital control logic — from elevator controllers and traffic lights to protocol parsers (TCP/IP, USB, SPI) and CPU instruction control units — is mathematically formalized as a Finite State Machine (FSM). Mastering Mealy and Moore machine architectures, state minimization, and race-free state assignment is the cornerstone of advanced digital system design.

◆ 1. Mealy vs. Moore State Machine Models

ParameterMoore MachineMealy Machine
Output DependencyDepends ONLY on the present state: $Y = f(S)$Depends on BOTH present state and current inputs: $Y = f(S, X)$
Output TimingChanges synchronously with clock edge (glitch-free)Changes asynchronously whenever input changes (can produce glitches)
State CountGenerally requires more states for the same specificationGenerally requires fewer states (often 1 state fewer than Moore)
Response SpeedReacts to inputs one clock cycle laterReacts to inputs immediately within the current clock cycle
State Bubble LabelState name / Output (e.g. $S_0 / 0$)State name only ($S_0$); Output placed on transition arrow ($X / Y$)

◆ 2. Systematic FSM Design Flow

  1. State Diagram Formulation: Translate verbal specifications into states, transitions, and outputs.
  2. State Table Construction: Tabulate Present State, Inputs, Next State, and Outputs.
  3. State Reduction:
    • Row Elimination: Two states $S_i$ and $S_j$ are equivalent if they produce identical outputs for all input combinations AND their next states are identical or equivalent.
    • Implication Table Method: Systematic pair-wise compatibility matrix to find all equivalent state pairs.
  4. State Assignment: Encode symbolic states into binary flip-flop variables ($Q_1, Q_0$):
    • Binary Encoding: $n$ flip-flops encode $2^n$ states (minimal flip-flops).
    • Gray Encoding: Adjacent states differ by 1 bit (minimizes switching noise).
    • One-Hot Encoding: Uses 1 flip-flop per state (e.g., 4 states $\to 0001, 0010, 0100, 1000$). Extremely fast decoding, ideal for FPGAs with abundant flip-flops.
  5. Next-State and Output Equations: Synthesize logic using K-maps for chosen flip-flop type (typically D flip-flops where $D = Q_{next}$).

◆ Worked Example: Non-Overlapping '101' Sequence Detector (Mealy)

Problem: Design a Mealy sequence detector with input $X$ and output $Z$ that outputs $Z = 1$ whenever the bit sequence $101$ is detected (non-overlapping).

Solution:
Define states based on history:
• $S_0$: Reset state (no bits matched).
• $S_1$: Got '1'.
• $S_2$: Got '10'.
Transitions:
• From $S_0$: if $X=0 \to S_0 (Z=0)$; if $X=1 \to S_1 (Z=0)$.
• From $S_1$: if $X=0 \to S_2 (Z=0)$; if $X=1 \to S_1 (Z=0)$ (retain latest '1').
• From $S_2$: if $X=0 \to S_0 (Z=0)$ (broken sequence '100'); if $X=1 \to S_0 (Z=1)$ (sequence completed! Non-overlapping routes back to $S_0$).
State assignment: 3 states $\implies 2$ D flip-flops ($Q_1, Q_0$). Let $S_0=00, S_1=01, S_2=10$, unused $= 11$.
Next-state equations from K-maps:
• $D_1 = Q_0 \\cdot \\bar{X}$
• $D_0 = \\bar{Q}_1 \\cdot \\bar{Q}_0 \\cdot X + \\bar{Q}_1 \\cdot Q_0 \\cdot X = \\bar{Q}_1 X$
• Output $Z = Q_1 \\cdot X$. ✓

Common mistake: Confusing overlapping and non-overlapping sequence detection. For overlapping '101' detection on input 10101, the detector outputs 00101 (two detections). For non-overlapping, it resets after each detection, producing 00100 (one detection).
Placement trap: "Why can Mealy machine outputs produce false transient spikes (glitches)?" — Because Mealy outputs are directly connected to inputs through combinational logic without a synchronizing register. Any intermediate glitch on input $X$ immediately propagates to output $Z$ during the clock cycle.

◆ Interview Questions

"Why is One-Hot state encoding preferred in FPGA designs while Binary encoding is preferred in ASIC designs?" — FPGAs are rich in D flip-flops and lookup tables (LUTs); One-Hot encoding assigns one flip-flop per state, making the next-state logic just a simple OR gate of predecessor transitions (fast timing closure). In custom ASICs, flip-flops consume significant silicon area, so designers minimize flip-flop count using compact binary or Gray state encoding.

Before Programmable Logic Devices, digital circuits required dozens of standard 7400-series TTL/CMOS SSI/MSI ICs interconnected on complex, error-prone printed circuit boards. PLDs revolutionized electronics by allowing engineers to implement custom multi-output combinational and sequential circuits on a single programmable silicon chip, reducing board area, propagation delay, and inventory cost.

◆ 1. The Three Classic PLD Architectures
